hints: With at most 12 numbers there are only 2<sup>12</sup> = 4096 subsets. Can you list them all? And as a bonus, look at one bit position at a time: in how many subsets does it end up switched on?

Enumerate subsets with recursion (take or skip each number) or bitmasks, XOR as you go and add each total. Shortcut: any bit that appears in at least one number is set in exactly half of all subsets, so the answer is (OR of all) · 2n−1.

1. Compute orAll = OR of every number.
  2. Each set bit of orAll is on in exactly 2n−1 of the 2n subsets.
  3. Return orAll shifted left by n−1.
  4. (Brute alternative: loop mask from 0 to 2n−1, XOR the chosen numbers, add to a sum.)

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Loop over all 2<sup>n</sup> masks; for each, XOR the chosen numbers and add the result.

approaches.name: Better
approaches.idea: Recursion that carries the running XOR (take or skip each element), so each subset costs O(1).

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Bit counting: a bit present in any number is on in exactly half the subsets, so the sum is OR(nums) · 2<sup>n−1</sup>.

explain: Sample [4,1]: OR is 5 (binary 101) and n = 2, so the answer is 5 · 2 = 10. Check by listing: subsets give 0, 4, 1 and 4^1 = 5, summing to 10. Why half? Pick a number that has the bit set; pairing every subset with the same subset with that number toggled flips the bit, so exactly half of the subsets have it on. Edge case: a bit that no number has contributes nothing, which the OR handles.
recognize: 'Sum of XOR over all subsets' with tiny n → enumerate subsets (bitmasks / recursion), or notice each bit is on in half of them.
javascript: function subsetXorSum(nums) { let o = 0; for (const x of nums) o |= x; return o * (1 << (nums.length - 1)); }
